title: Midnight weight-stitch heuristic failure and mitigation notes
body:
Summary:

On 2026-03-10 at ~00:45 UTC we observed a small but noisy increase in model decode errors and token alignment anomalies from a canary cohort during a midnight rollout. The canary set comprised ~1% of traffic across two regions. The anomaly surfaced as a shift in decoded text for long-context prompts (responses contained repeated or missing tokens near shard boundaries), raising error rates on our QA prompts and triggering regression alerts from the quality monitor. No user-visible outage was reported beyond degraded quality on a few test routes.

Why this doc exists:

This is an on-call investigation log + initial post-incident notes capturing timeline, root-cause hypothesis, immediate mitigations, and recommended runbook/run-preflight changes. The rollout used the new "weight-stitch heuristic" (PR referenced above) intended to reduce memory spikes during incremental weight apply by heuristically concatenating small contiguous shards. The heuristic was intended to be a no-op for canonical full-model swaps but was exercised by our incremental-weight-path handling.

Detection and signals:

- 00:45 UTC: Quality regression alert (eval-runner) flagged +12% failure on the long-context prompt suite for model variant: v2.7-quant.
- 00:47 UTC: Canary service-level monitor p95 latency stable, but token-level decode error rate increased to 0.9% (baseline 0.02%).
- 00:50 UTC: Ops Slack thread #canary-alert auto-created; on-call SRE paged.
- 01:05 UTC: Internal smoke tests reproduced token shift locally when running the exact deployed artifact and manifest.

Immediate actions taken (timeline):

- 01:10 UTC: Paused rollout in the orchestration plane (prevented additional hosts from receiving the incremental apply).
- 01:18 UTC: Forced canary hosts to serve the previously pinned model version by re-issuing the full-weight-apply (fallback path) on the two canary instances; observed immediate reduction in decode anomalies.
- 01:40 UTC: Rolled back the weight-stitch heuristic merge (reverted runtime flag in prod config) and triggered a staged re-apply to remaining canaries under validation.
- 02:30 UTC: Confirmed QA evals returned to baseline on canaries and lifted the pause.

Investigation notes and evidence collected:

- Repro steps: Running our smoke harness with the exact deployed wheel and the manifest produced the token alignment shift on the local harness but not when running a contiguous full-weight-apply flow.
- Hashes and checksums: Model manifest SHA matched expected, but per-shard byte-order checksums after incremental-stitch differed between hosts that applied the heuristic path and hosts that used the fallback path.
- Logs: Stitching logs (runtime DEBUG) showed non-deterministic ordering when assembling patch shards: the code used Python dict iteration over a map of shard IDs during a composition step; in some runs the insertion order differed under high-concurrency scheduling leading to different final contiguous tensors across hosts.
- Symptom mapping: The decode shift correlated tightly with shard-boundary token sequences in our synthetic prompts; embedding rows appearing off-by-one at a shard boundary produced predictable token mis-emissions for rare token ids near the tail of vocabulary segments.

Root cause hypothesis (most-likely):

A non-deterministic shard concatenation order in the incremental weight-stitching heuristic caused the assembled model tensors to differ across hosts. These ordering differences are subtle (only at shard boundaries) and do not affect checks on total manifest SHA, but they alter the mapping of embedding matrix rows to token indices when shards are concatenated inconsistently. This produced a token-id offset for tokens falling at the affected boundaries, causing decode shift and quality regressions only under long-context prompts that exercise those embeddings.

Why checks did not catch it earlier:

- Pre-rollout checks validated manifest-level SHA (unchanged) and per-shard file sizes, but we did not compute a post-apply deterministic row-level checksum or verify ordering across hosts after incremental applies.
- Unit tests for the stitching code assumed stable iteration order; they missed concurrency interleavings that appear under production-like parallel apply scheduling.

Short-term mitigations applied (what we did):

- Rollback of the runtime config flag enabling the heuristic across all rolling hosts.
- Forced full-weight-apply fallback on the two canary hosts that saw anomalies to align their in-memory tensors.
- Added a temporary post-apply verification job that computes per-row checksums for embeddings and compares them to the authoritative canonical assembly (in S3). This job runs as a blocking health check for canaries for the next 72 hours.

Planned long-term fixes and runbook updates:

1) Determinism fixes (engineering):
   - Modify the stitching implementation to explicitly sort shard IDs before concatenation (deterministic order) and add concurrent-apply resilience (e.g., lock-free compare-and-swap with ordered composition). (Owner: eng-serving-runtime)
   - Add CI tests that run heavy parallel apply scenarios with randomized scheduling for the incremental path. (Owner: eng-serving-runtime)

2) Runtime verification (sre + eng):
   - Add a post-apply per-shard row-level checksum verification that runs automatically after any incremental apply and fails the host health check if mismatched. (Owner: eng-site-reliability)
   - Extend the canary preflight to include a "model-assembly identity" step that verifies per-host assembly deterministic fingerprint before routing production traffic. (Owner: product-hosted-api)

3) Rollout policy changes (product + SRE):
   - For any change touching weight-apply/stitch paths, require a two-stage canary: first stage applies to a zero-traffic canary cluster with post-apply checksum verification; second stage opens traffic if checks pass for 24 hours. (Owner: release-engineering)
   - Add an explicit QA prompt set that targets known shard-boundary tokens to the standard canary eval suite. (Owner: applied-ml)

4) Runbook updates (SRE):
   - Add a troubleshooting checklist: how to detect ordering mismatches, how to compute per-row checksums, commands to force fallback full-apply, and escalation path to runtime engineers.
   - Create a quick command alias in the ops tooling to compute and compare post-apply assembly fingerprints across a set of hosts. (Owner: eng-sre)

Follow-ups and owners (action item list):

- ENG-SERVING-RUNTIME: PR to sort shard IDs + unit tests (due 2026-03-17) - Marcus Lee.
- ENG-SERVING-RUNTIME: Add randomized parallel apply CI job (due 2026-03-24) - Priya Shah.
- ENG-SRE: Implement blocking post-apply checksum health-check for 72-hour window (done temporary); permanent implementation due 2026-03-20 - Aisha Patel.
- RELEASE-ENG: Update rollout policy checklist and add two-stage canary gating (due 2026-03-19) - Diego Martinez.
- APPLIED-ML: Add shard-boundary QA prompts to standard suite (due 2026-03-22) - Eshita Rao.

Open questions and unknowns:

- Were there any other heuristics in the same release that rely on unordered maps? We should scan the release diff for similar patterns.
- Is it possible that quantized packing of shards exacerbated the symptom? Early indications say effect is ordering-only, but further fuzzing required.

Notes to on-call and SREs:

- If you encounter a similar canary-quality regression again: immediately pause rollout, check per-shard post-apply fingerprints (new temporary job), and if mismatch detected, force full-weight-apply fallback on affected hosts. Escalate to eng-serving-runtime if assembly fingerprints differ but sizes match.
- Avoid restarting hosts repeatedly while an incremental apply is in-flight; instead, force an abort of the incremental job and requeue a full apply.
- Use the alias commands added to the ops repo: ops/model-assembly-check --hosts <hostlist> and ops/force-full-apply --hosts <hostlist>.

Appendix: quick commands (examples)

- Compute assembly fingerprint on host: sudo /opt/runtime/bin/assembly-fingerprint /var/model/current > /tmp/fingerprint.txt
- Compare with canonical: aws s3 cp s3://models/canonical/v2.7/fingerprint.txt /tmp/canonical.txt && diff /tmp/fingerprint.txt /tmp/canonical.txt
- Force full apply: ops/force-full-apply --host <id> --manifest s3://models/canonical/v2.7/manifest.json

Slack threads, PRs and tickets referenced:

- GH: redwood-inference/runtime#4921 (weight-stitch heuristic)
- JIRA: SRE-1873 (canary regression incident)
- Confluence: Rollouts/WeightApplyGuidelines (existing guidance to be updated)

Closing note:

This was a low-severity but informative incident demonstrating how non-determinism in an optimization path can quietly bypass coarse preflight checks. The immediate rollback and fallback path behaved as expected; the focus now is on hardening determinism, adding portable verification, and adjusting rollout gates so that future incremental-weight optimizations cannot slip past host-level identity checks.

Document owner/contact: Aisha Patel (eng-site-reliability)

Last updated: 2026-03-12 14:18 UTC
